title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

reading.body:
This is an insider misuse case, not a model error. A person with legitimate access to law enforcement systems is alleged to have used them for a purpose they were not deployed for: tracking a specific individual without her consent. The systems named, a Flock camera system, a tag reader system, and the Georgia Crime Information Center database, are built for policing, and the alleged misuse happened inside that authorised access rather than through any break in the technology.

The failure sits at the point where access controls meet the person holding them. Nothing in the reporting suggests the systems malfunctioned or produced false output. What is alleged is that a sworn officer directed ordinary system functions at a private end, which means the detection would have to come from audit trails, query logging, or a complaint rather than from the software refusing the request. The investigation here began after the sheriff requested it, and it took a multi-year state inquiry to produce an indictment.

The charges are allegations. An indictment is not a conviction, and the reporting does not establish guilt, intent, or what internal oversight, if any, flagged the alleged queries before the woman came forward.

reports.title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

summary:
A former Coffee County sheriff's deputy, Chris Ashley Rozar, 49, was released on bond on May 5 after a grand jury indicted him on eight counts. The charges include four counts of violating his oath as a public officer, two counts of computer invasion of privacy, one count of prohibited use of captured license plate data, and one count of stalking. Prosecutors allege he misused the sheriff's office Flock camera system, tag reader system, and the Georgia Crime Information Center database for personal reasons, including tracking and surveilling a woman without her consent between April 10 and May 1, 2024.

The woman, who spoke anonymously to WALB, said she hopes her story encourages other women to report abuse. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation led the multi-year investigation, which began in 2024 after then-Sheriff Doyle Wooten requested it, and Rozar was fired when it started. He was arrested on May 5 and is scheduled for arraignment on May 27 in Coffee County Superior Court.
